name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
study_type: experimental (flight experiment on the ISS), with normal-gravity laboratory tests
investigators_note: University project scientist: Yu-Chien (Alice) Chien (UC Irvine). Co-Investigators: Felix Weinberg (Imperial College London, died 2012) and Sunny Karnani. Lead collaborator: Sergey Minaev (Far Eastern Federal University). NASA science team: Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam (CWRU); Fumiaki Takahashi was deputy project scientist for drop testing.
objective: Gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how an electric field (ion-driven wind) can be used to control non-premixed flames. Specific objectives: (A) determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel (methane, ethylene) flow rate and nitrogen dilution; (B) obtain the time response of flame chemiluminescence, luminosity and ion current to large step changes in voltage; (C) evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (soot volume fraction and location of luminous soot) in relation to field voltage and ion current; (D) use the ion current vs. voltage behavior to characterize near-limit lifted flames and use the ion-driven wind to stabilize or reattach them.
hypothesis: Electric fields applied in microgravity will strongly influence laminar diffusion flames, allowing flame stability, soot behavior and combustion to be controlled through the ion-driven wind and chemi-ionization.
approach: A voltage of up to 10 kV, of either sign, was applied between the burner and a copper mesh above it. In each test a flame was ignited, allowed to settle, and the voltage was swept in small steps or ramps while ion current, light emission and images were recorded. Round 1 (March to May 2018) used the coflow burner with and without a weak air flow; round 2 (September to November 2018) used a simple gas-jet burner. Fuels were methane and ethylene, pure or diluted with nitrogen. Tests were commanded from the ground with scripts.
geometry: Laminar non-premixed jet flames on the axis of the 0.4 m diameter ACME chamber insert, with a flat circular copper mesh electrode downstream of the burner. (1) Coflow burner (same as CLD Flame): stainless fuel tube ID 2.16 mm (nominal 2.2 mm), OD 2.41 mm, protruding 3.1 mm beyond the annulus outlet; outer tube ID 25 mm; annulus outlet is a 6.4 mm thick Hastelloy X honeycomb (0.81 mm cells, 0.05 mm foil). Mesh 37 mm above the fuel tube outlet (alternate position 52 mm, not used). (2) Gas-jet burner ('2.1 mm'): same tubing, ID 2.16 mm, OD 2.41 mm, mesh nominally 35 mm downstream. Mesh: 8.9 cm diameter with copper ring (8.4 cm without), square copper weave of 7.1 wires/cm, 0.43 mm wire diameter, 48% open area. Retractable resistively heated hot-wire igniter with crew-exchangeable tip and stepper-motor radial drive.
conditions_note: Chamber atmosphere and coflow were synthetic air (21 % O2, 79 % N2 by volume) in all tests, at a nominal 100 kPa (14.5 psi). Pressure was measured but per-test values are not in the PSI table. Tests are constant-volume, so pressure rises slightly and oxygen falls during a test. ambient_temperature_K = 298 is a nominal value (cabin room temperature, about 25 °C), assumed by the team; it was not measured or reported for these tests.
flow: Coflow burner tests with a weak coflow of synthetic air (21/79 O2/N2 by volume), e.g. 3.1 cm/s, or with no coflow (0 cm/s); gas-jet burner tests with the fuel jet issuing into the quiescent chamber atmosphere (same synthetic air). Fuel jet velocities of e.g. 15, 19 and 27 cm/s. The applied field drives an ion wind upward (mesh negative, positive ions toward the mesh) or toward the burner (mesh positive), which can push the flame down onto the burner.
gravity_note: ISS, with comparison tests in normal gravity
hardware_note: ACME chamber insert in the Combustion Integrated Rack (chamber about 100 L, about 90 L free), with the coflow or gas-jet burner, retracting igniter, high-voltage power supplies (one polarity installed at a time) and a removable copper mesh electrode 35 to 37 mm above the burner.
sensors: High-voltage power supply and ion-current measurement (mesh potential and chemi-ion current through the flame (V–I curves))
ACME data camera (DataCam) (flame shape, luminosity, soot location; color-ratio soot pyrometry and soot volume fraction)
Intensified monochrome camera (CH* chemiluminescence imaging (reaction-zone location))
HiBMs camera with collimated illumination (soot volume fraction by light extinction)
Analog color operations camera (flame behavior during operations)
Photomultiplier tube (PMT) modules (x3) (OH* (310 nm), CH* and broadband (neutral-density filtered) emission vs time)
Chamber pressure and temperature sensors (chamber pressure and gas temperature)
Mass flow controllers (x3) (fuel, N2 dilution and coflow air flow rates)
measured_or_computed_quantities: ion current as a function of applied voltage (V-I curve)
field strength at peak ion current
OH*, CH* and broad-band light emission
chamber pressure and temperature, gas flow rates
key_results: In microgravity the V-I curve shows a distinct ion-current peak at the most compact flame, then a drop to a lower saturation plateau; 1-g flames rise smoothly to saturation.
Peak ion current is roughly proportional to fuel flow velocity and increases with coflow; it is higher in microgravity than in comparable 1-g flames.
The electric body force can produce flame oscillations similar to buoyant flicker, and microgravity flames under a field can mimic 1-g flame shapes.
With the gas-jet burner and an upward ion wind the V-I curve is parabolic, unlike the coflow burner; reversing polarity does not give an inverted result.
Soot plus electric field gives complex behavior: soot elimination, showers of incandescent particles, unstable 'dancing' flames, and soot deposits on the burner and mesh.
space_benefits: Not aimed at a space application, but the findings could help future space combustion devices, for example for solid waste processing.
earth_benefits: Electric fields could allow stable, leaner burner operation with less soot and pollutant emission, and more efficient combustion.
scenario_relevance: NOT FILLED IN (to be computed from the team's ranking rules). Note: All tests in 21 % O2 near 1 atm, with gas fuels on a burner. It adds understanding of flame control by electric fields, not flammability limits.

data_quality_notes: O2: the chamber atmosphere and the coflow were synthetic air, 21% O2 / 79% N2 by volume, in all tests (no O2 variation). Some vitiation occurs during each constant-volume test.

Pressure: nominal 100 kPa (14.5 psi) in the final report; pressure was measured (chamber pressure sensor) but per-test values are not in the experimental table. The CIR chamber can operate up to 300 kPa.

Hardware changes before flight: the 1.3 mm jet burner was dropped (fall 2016); coflow-burner tests were added to compensate for the slow HVPS; polarity switching within a test was dropped because of electromagnetic interference.
Thin Filament Pyrometry (14 µm SiC fibers) was not used because the fibers interfere with the electric field.

Anomalies: IPSU-G drive failure (2018-04-27, recovered 2018-05-07); IPSU-1/HiBMs unavailable on 2018-09-26 and 2018-10-01; heavy soot deposited on the coflow burner after the last positive-mesh ethylene day (2018-05-17), cleaned by the crew on 2018-06-19; MFC flow oscillations.
The last test day (2018-11-15, 100% C2H4 bottle diluted to 25/50/80/100%) appears twice in the PSI experimental table; it is counted once (11 flames).
ambient_temperature_K = 298 is nominal (assumed), not a measurement.
